sources.title: The Term Spread and the Case of the Missing 2024 Recession

discussion.body: So the curve may never have been the alarm — the debt service ratio was the thing actually ringing.
Maybe not either/or. The curve could signal that growth is slowing, while the debt-service burden decides whether slowing turns into an actual recession.
Either way, anyone who wrote off the term spread entirely after 2024 is over-correcting from a single miss.

items.title: The 2022 Inversion Promised a Recession. 2024 Didn't Deliver One.
items.body: Yield-curve inversion has long been treated as the closest thing to a recession alarm. After the large and persistent inversion of 2022, most term-spread measures — 10-year minus 3-month, 10-year minus 2-year — flagged a high likelihood of recession in 2023-24. No recession arrived in 2024, and that miss has forced a reappraisal of the measure's reputation as the most reliable US recession predictor. A new paper by Laurent Ferrara and coauthors, “Missing Recessions: Revisiting the Term Spread's Predictive Power,” reports that adding the debt service ratio to the model reconciles the false alarm for both the US and Germany, following the approach of Borio and colleagues (2020). That leaves an open interpretive question: does the curve carry information of its own, or does it largely stand proxy for the debt burden that does the real work?

sources.title: Ontario to import U.S. electricity this winter, months after Ford threatened to cut power exports

items.title: Ontario Will Import U.S. Electricity This Winter, Months After Ford Threatened to Cut Exports
items.body: Ontario's independent electricity operator has announced that the province will import power from the United States this winter. That comes just a few months after Premier Doug Ford threatened to cut Ontario's exports to the U.S. amid the ongoing trade war. Same grid, same trading partner, opposite direction — a reminder that cross-border electricity is a bargaining chip right up until a season arrives that needs megawatts.

discussion.body: The asymmetry is the story: an issue can vanish from national coverage and still decide governor's races.
Small caution — voters ranking cost of living higher in polls doesn't mean abortion stops mattering to them, just that it competes with other concerns.
Which is consistent with a partial retreat rather than a reversal.

items.title: Republican Governor Candidates Are Backing Away From Some Abortion Positions
items.body: Republican candidates for governor are walking back some of their abortion stances, according to PBS NewsHour. The retreat, in its account, points at an incentive problem: reproductive rights have faded from the national spotlight and polls show voters far more likely to prioritize cost-of-living concerns, yet the political ramifications of pushing for new abortion restrictions remain substantial. Falling off the national agenda and falling off voters' priority lists are not the same thing.

items.title: John Wilson Has Been Filming Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden Since August
items.body: Variety reports that John Wilson has been rolling cameras on Harry Styles at Madison Square Garden since August, citing two sources. Wilson is the director behind the indie box-office surprise “The History of Concrete” and HBO's “How To with John Wilson,” and the trade calls Styles's Garden residency historic while describing the filmmaker as one of the buzziest documentarians on the market, invited behind the curtain by Styles himself. A residency is a useful shape for a documentary — a fixed venue, a long run, a set of routines that repeat and slowly change — which may be why the pairing reads as more than a tour souvenir.

discussion.body: The template is legible: one earnest young narrator, one enormous moral or historical mess, and a tone that keeps the mess at arm's length.

A haul of awards and a big gross don't settle whether the second pass holds up. The critic applying that yardstick already calls the first film crass and mawkish, and the same instincts could read as shtick when repeated.
That's the interesting part: the criticism and the hardware aim at the same qualities — a child's-eye tone blunt enough to make hard material bearable, and blunt enough to annoy.

items.title: Waititi's Adaptation Move: Shrink the Novel to a Child's Eye
items.body: Variety's review of “Klara and the Sun” frames Taika Waititi's new film as a repeat of a move that worked once before: taking a solemn, complex, questioning novel and turning it into a cockeyed child's-eye comedy. The precedent the review reaches for is “Jojo Rabbit” — described as a crass, mawkish anti-hate satire about a Hitler Youth member's personal and political awakening — which won Waititi an Oscar and grossed nearly $100 million, in spite of what the reviewer calls its manifold artistic problems. The mechanism is a perspective trick rather than a plot device. Serious material filtered through a narrator who takes the world at face value can be carried without being fully comprehended, which is a way of holding a heavy subject at an angle. It is also, in the reviewer's own language, a style that reads as crass and mawkish when the balance tips — the Oscar and the box office arrive next to the criticism, not instead of it.

items.body: The major-party candidates for Minnesota's U.S. Senate seat faced off in an hourlong debate on MPR News, with fraud, affordability and the fallout from the Trump administration's policies as the points of friction, NPR reports. The three themes sit in different registers: an allegation-centered fight, household costs, and a set of federal decisions a senator would have little direct control over but plenty of reason to take a position on.

sources.title: Paul McCartney Was Concerned Paul Mescal Is “Markedly Shorter” Than ‘The Beatles’ Co-Stars

items.title: Paul McCartney's One Casting Note for the Beatles Biopic: Height
items.body: Sam Mendes' upcoming Beatles biopic will take audiences back to Abbey Road, and Paul McCartney has a note about the casting. He said he was concerned that Paul Mescal looks “markedly shorter” than his co-stars, Deadline reports, and that he even reached out to Mendes about it — though he doesn't know how the director is addressing it. It is a very specific worry, and a revealing one: a band is a set of silhouettes as much as it is a set of voices, and the four Beatles' proportions are part of an image fixed in memory. Not every director treats a lineup as a composition. McCartney apparently does.

items.title: Kylie Minogue Nearly Brought Cammy Back to Street Fighter
items.body: Kylie Minogue's turn as Cammy — bazooka included — won over Street Fighter fans more than 30 years ago. Deadline reports she nearly returned for a cameo in the newly released Paramount adaptation, and that the lobbying came from Orville Peck, who plays Vega in the film and is a friend and collaborator of the Australian singer. Peck said he was trying to make it happen. Near-miss cameos are their own genre of film trivia, but this one has a better origin than most: the veteran was being courted by a castmate with her phone number, not by a studio marketing plan.

sources.title: Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia show the Yemeni rebels' growing strength

discussion.body: The uncomfortable reading is about the limits of air power: you can hit a movement for ten years and still be describing its growth.

Or the raids were never really aimed at defeating it. Punishment and signalling are different goals, and judging a campaign by whether the Houthis ended up smaller could be answering a question nobody was asking.

items.title: PBS on a Decade of Air Raids: The Houthis Grew Stronger
items.body: PBS NewsHour's account of the war in Yemen is blunt about what a decade of air power has produced. At various times over the last decade, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, the United States, Britain and Israel have carried out punishing air raids on the Houthis, it reports — only to see the rebels grow even stronger. Five states, one target, and a movement that emerges from the bombardment looking more formidable than before. That record is worth keeping in mind whenever airstrikes are described as a way of settling a fight with an entrenched armed group: as descriptions of results, “punishing” and “effective” are not synonyms.

sources.title: 2 seriously hurt, 11 others injured in B.C. crash that shut down Highway 99

items.title: Police First Reported No Serious Injuries. The Late Update Said Two Were Seriously Hurt.
items.body: Surrey police initially reported no serious injuries in a crash. Late Friday night, the force said two of the injured were seriously hurt and that one was airlifted to hospital. Short of a medical assessment, a first report from a crash scene tends to be provisional — and this one moved within hours, in the direction of worse news.

discussion.body: Nobody staring at a grocery receipt needs an ad to tell them prices are up. The ads are competing to supply the explanation for why.
Or the spending buys repetition rather than explanation. A campaign can saturate a market and still lose the argument about the price of eggs.

items.title: Ten Billion Dollars of Campaign Ads, and a Grocery Bill
items.body: NPR's perspective segment puts two facts in the same sentence: campaign ad spending has topped $10 billion this election cycle, and voters are struggling to afford groceries and gas. It doesn't have to claim one causes the other — the adjacency is the argument. That is what the political system treats as abundant, spent in front of households doing daily arithmetic on a shopping list.

The genre matters, but the more useful question may be why the attacks keep returning to one member in particular rather than to her arguments.

Insults aimed at a legislator's person rather than her votes are their own kind of argument: they ask supporters to react to the woman instead of the record.

sources.title: Offshoring and Voting Patterns in the US

items.title: Offshoring and the Ballot: a Central Bank Paper's Question
items.body: The Bank of Canada has published a paper studying the impact of offshoring by US firms on voting patterns for incumbents in the US. The pairing is what makes it interesting: a firm's decision to move work abroad, and the electoral fate of the politicians who happen to be in office when it happens. If voters do connect the two, the politics of trade is not only about prices and jobs; it is also about who catches the blame.

discussion.body: The word doing the heavy lifting is 'upended.' Two studies can destabilise a research programme without closing the question of how much emotional expression is shared across cultures.

Fair, but the colonial angle is not a footnote you can bracket off. If the universalist picture carried those assumptions, the case for universality has to be rebuilt without them rather than just restated.

items.title: Are Emotions Universal? The Colonial Critique Attached to the Question
items.body: Psyche puts the question plainly: are our emotions universal? A video by Then & Now argues that two landmark studies upended the prevailing view of emotions, and that in doing so they challenged colonial stereotypes. Those two halves belong together. A theory holding that a given expression means the same thing everywhere is also a claim about whose emotional life supplies the baseline for everyone else. Saying the older picture carried colonial assumptions does not by itself settle how much of emotional life is shared and how much is learned, but it changes what is at stake in the answer: the argument stops being only about what faces do and becomes one about who defined the default.
